name: Ruth Mountain and Icy Peak Traverse
region: North Cascades National Park, Hannegan Pass

legs.route: Hannegan Pass to the glacier and up the snow to the summit
Ruth–Icy ridge to the saddle below Icy, then the snow and final rock gully to the northwest summit
legs.connect: Follow the divide south from Ruth, drop through a steep snow gully to the low point of the ridge, then continue along the divide to the saddle below Icy.

how: Climbers walk to Hannegan Pass, then climb Ruth over snow and glacier, usually on the first day. Bivy sites sit at the notch on Ruth's west ridge and on the saddle near the small north-facing glacier below Icy. The link to Icy follows the divide and includes a steep snow gully of about 40 degrees; early in the season the glacier below Icy has a few crevasses. The last stretch to the summit is a short rock gully on the south side of the northwest summit, third class. A glacier kit with ice axe and crampons is the extra over a simple Ruth climb.
descent: Return along the divide back toward Hannegan Pass, or reverse the route over Ruth, then walk out the trail. Ski parties have skied off Icy and re-climbed Ruth's south ridge to finish.
logistics: The route lies inside the national park, so an overnight stay needs a backcountry permit from the ranger station. Best on early-summer snow; late in the season the glaciers open up and the gullies lose their snow.
notes: Mountaineers route pages (403) and WTA reports exist but were not readable; class 3 final gully from the 2016 ranger report; one-day ski version from the 2003 report.

name: Snowfield, Neve and Colonial from the Neve Col camp
region: North Cascades, Colonial Creek / Pyramid Lake

legs.route: Neve Glacier and the west ridge
Short climb from the Neve Col camp
legs.connect: Return to camp, then climb the short slope from the col to the summit.

legs.route: Colonial Glacier to the west or east summit
legs.connect: From camp cross the Colonial Glacier toward the notch and climb the peak; the higher summit is the east one, easy to mix up with the west.

how: Climbers walk the Pyramid Lake trail, leave it on the steep climbers' path to the ridge, then traverse under the cliffs of Pyramid Peak and cross the Colonial Glacier to the col between Colonial and Neve. Camp there. Snowfield is the long day: rope up for the Neve Glacier, then follow rock and a knife-edge ridge on the upper west side with some class 4. Neve is a short evening climb from camp and Colonial fits into the following morning. Some parties also add Paul Bunyan's Stump.
descent: Return to camp, then reverse the approach across the Colonial Glacier, the traverse under Pyramid's cliffs, and the climbers' path back to the trail.
logistics: Camping in the national park needs a permit. The traverse below Pyramid is exposed to rockfall and avalanche, so cross it in the cool of the morning. Late-season glaciers are open with thin snow bridges.
notes: One 2013 party climbed Pyramid and Horseman's Pack too and camped beside the Colonial Glacier; guide pages cite a 3-day Snowfield-Neve-Colonial schedule (Mountaineers pages 403). One 12-hour day trip to Snowfield alone is reported.

name: Saska, Emerald and Cardinal Peaks

legs.route: Snow slopes to the south ridge, then class 3 along the crest
Gully and ribs, mostly easy scrambling
legs.connect: Traverse back across the basin to the foot of Emerald and climb moderate slopes.

legs.route: Snowfield and slabs from the basin
legs.connect: Descend and cross the basin to Cardinal's base, then cut steps up the snowfield to the slabs.

how: From the Entiat River road the approach is a long day with heavy packs to a meadow camp below Cardinal. The three peaks are done as one circuit from that camp, Saska first, then Emerald, then Cardinal. Saska has class 3 scrambling along a narrow ridge. Emerald is the easiest of the three. Cardinal's slabs are the most committing part and feel tricky in boots. Climbers sometimes add Pinnacle Mountain via a nearby pass.
descent: Each peak is descended to the shared basin, using snowfields where they last. Camp is struck the next day and the approach is reversed.
logistics: The last miles of the access road are often closed, which adds walking. Early-season snow helps the gullies; bring crampons and an axe in spring.
notes: Reports differ on order and on whether Pinnacle is included; a winter ski version did Cardinal, Emerald, Saska in one day from a Grouse Creek bivy. Saska: class 3 (two reports) vs class 2 via the southeast ridge (one); higher kept.

name: Mount Spickard and Mount Redoubt from the Ouzel Lake camp

legs.route: South ridge via the small glacier and the 8000 ft col
Redoubt Glacier and the south face
legs.connect: Return to camp, then take a second day up the Redoubt Glacier.

how: The Depot Creek approach starts near the border and climbs a headwall with a fixed line to a camp at Ouzel Lake. Both peaks are climbed from that camp on separate days. Spickard needs a glacier crossing at about 30 to 35 degrees, then class 3 gullies and a chimney to the top. Redoubt needs roped glacier travel to a col south of the Flying Buttress, then snow and ice, class 4 rock and an exposed traverse. Parties often add Custer or Rahm as well.
descent: Both summits are descended by reversing the climb; on Redoubt that includes a short downclimb and a step lowered on webbing.
logistics: A high-clearance 4x4 helps on the access road. Best early to mid summer with the glaciers still covered; rockfall and soft snow make Redoubt risky later in the day.
notes: Order varies: one report did Redoubt first. Spickard also done via its north glacier by ski parties.

name: Maude, Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow (Entiat Cirque)
region: Entiat Mountains, Phelps Creek / Leroy Basin

legs.route: From the col below the summit up talus and scree
Climbers' path from Leroy Basin then talus to the summit
legs.connect: Descend from Maude to Leroy Basin and climb the path and talus up Seven Fingered Jack. The ridge between the two is technical and normally skipped.

legs.route: Southwest slope from the pass west of Seven Fingered Jack
legs.connect: Cross the pass beside Seven Fingered Jack, pass the tarn, and climb ledges and slabs; the final ledges are class 4.

how: Start at the Phelps Creek trailhead and camp around Leroy Basin. Maude and Seven Fingered Jack are the easier two and can be done on the same day. Fernow is longer, needs route-finding on ledges and slabs with a snowfield above, and is often saved for the next day.
descent: Each peak is descended by its own route back to camp; going down Fernow's route is slow late in the season.
logistics: The Phelps Creek road is rough. Crampons and an axe are useful for the snowfield on Fernow and the Maude col.
notes: Only partly verified: several other pages (Mountaineers, cascadeclimbers, summitpost) were 403 or empty. A fast Fernow-7FJ-Maude one-day loop appears only in search snippets. Fernow class 4 final ledges from one trip.
